word:lxx:L700438.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to someone identified as Ailous or Elus. word:lxx:L700474.explanation: Aisam is a proper name for a person; the same name is also given as Esam. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. word:lxx:L700665.explanation: “Fisherman” refers to a person who catches fish. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is part of a literal description or a larger picture, but the word itself identifies the person engaged in catching fish.

word:lxx:L700809.explanation: This adjective describes something that has no separate parts and cannot be divided. It expresses the idea of unity as a whole rather than something assembled from pieces. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains “without parts; indivisible.”

word:lxx:L701204.explanation: This noun means “tolerance”: the willingness to endure or bear with something rather than respond with immediate rejection or resistance. It describes a capacity for patience or restraint, though its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:25. The available lexical meaning identifies the word clearly, while the verse reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text to explain the specific situation in which it is used.

word:lxx:L701248.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Antilibanos” or “Antilivanos.” It identifies a named place or geographical feature in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or person in general. word:lxx:L701330.explanation: Apaiteō means to demand back what belongs to you.

word:lxx:L701349.explanation: This adverb means “from above” or “from the top.” It describes direction or position, pointing to something that comes down from a higher place or is located at the upper part of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Job. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what object, place, or movement the surrounding words describe.

word:lxx:L701385.explanation: This verb means to refute thoroughly—to answer a claim by exposing it as wrong or unable to stand. It describes a strong, complete rebuttal rather than a brief disagreement. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and argument, but its central idea is a decisive refutation.

word:lxx:L701415.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that is “unapproachable” or “terrible”—not easily approached and inspiring fear or awe. It expresses a quality rather than an action, so its exact force depends on the person or thing it describes in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament translation represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:11. The word’s central sense remains the same: a presence so formidable that people shrink from coming near.

word:lxx:L701532.explanation: The verb means “attribute”: it describes assigning something to a person or source, crediting it to them rather than merely mentioning it. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone attributes something to someone or something else. This LXX word occurs three times in its corpus, appearing once in Deuteronomy and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L701688.explanation: Ararat is a proper name identifying a place called Ararat. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Genesis 8:4, 2 Kings 19:37, and Jeremiah 28:27. The word functions as a place-name rather than a general description, action, or quality. It points readers to a named location, while the surrounding passage determines why that location is mentioned. The word itself does not carry a broader abstract meaning in the information available here.

word:lxx:L701824.explanation: Artaxerxes is the name of a king.

word:lxx:L701868.explanation: Arōni, also written Aroni, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish further meaning or significance beyond identifying the person who bears it.

word:lxx:L701886.explanation: Asaraddōn; Asaraththon is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L701921.explanation: Asennaphar, also rendered Asennafar, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 4:10. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person’s role and significance there; the name itself functions as a personal designation rather than a general description.

word:lxx:L702014.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “urbane”—polished, cultivated, and socially refined. It points to a manner that is pleasant, well-mannered, or suited to respectable society rather than rough or unpolished. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus. Its exact force in any verse depends on the person or thing it describes and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L702058.explanation: “Aschōd; Askhoth” is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the genealogy’s immediate context, while the word itself functions as a specific name.

word:lxx:L702137.explanation: This noun means “courtyard” or “fold,” referring to an enclosed open area or a bounded place for animals. word:lxx:L702142.explanation: Aun, also rendered Avn, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. word:lxx:L702205.explanation: This word means “incorruptibility; integrity.” It names a quality of being uncorrupted and whole, describing what remains sound rather than spoiled, damaged, or compromised. As a noun, it refers to this quality itself, whether viewed as freedom from corruption or as complete moral and personal soundness. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea remains lasting incorruptibility and integrity.

word:lxx:L702353.explanation: This proper name means “Babylōnia” or “Vavilonia,” referring to Babylonia. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L702476.explanation: Balanas, also rendered Valanas, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role in that passage cannot be explained further; the lexical information establishes the name itself and its alternate rendering.

word:lxx:L702498.explanation: Bamōth, also rendered Vamoth, is a proper name for a place. word:lxx:L702887.explanation: Gazara is a proper name for a place, rendered “Gazara” in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. word:lxx:L703026.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “joking”—speaking or behaving in a playful, unserious way rather than treating something as a serious matter. word:lxx:L703084.explanation: This word is a proper name, identifying a named person or entity rather than describing an action or quality. word:lxx:L703141.explanation: This adjective describes something that is known or can be known. word:lxx:L703534.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “conclude”: to bring something to an end or complete it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. word:lxx:L703578.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “leap about.” It describes a person or thing moving through lively, active jumps rather than simply standing or walking. word:lxx:L703596.explanation: This noun means “breach” or “gap”: an opening where something has been broken, divided, or left incomplete. It names the break itself rather than an action. word:lxx:L703620.explanation: Diaphanēs means diaphanous, describing something transparent.

word:lxx:L703659.explanation: This verb means “peep out” or “lean out.” It describes someone looking or extending themselves outward from a place of concealment or enclosure, so the central idea is a cautious movement into view. word:lxx:L704139.explanation: This word means “centurion,” a noun naming a military officer. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 2 Kings 11:10 and 2 Kings 11:15. word:lxx:L704746.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “send in.” It describes the act of causing someone or something to enter or be placed inside. word:lxx:L704830.explanation: This verb means “buy out” or “make the most of,” describing an active effort to obtain the greatest possible use or advantage from an opportunity. word:lxx:L704849.explanation: This verb means “know accurately”: to possess clear, precise knowledge rather than a vague or mistaken understanding. word:lxx:L704885.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to adorn or deck out—to make something more attractive or suitably arranged by adding decoration. word:lxx:L704948.explanation: Exodos means an exodus—a departure or going out.

word:lxx:L705208.explanation: This adjective describes something as “laborious” or “tiring”—requiring effort, causing weariness, or being difficult to endure. word:lxx:L705244.explanation: This verb means “set a mark upon.” It describes placing a mark on something or someone, identifying or indicating it in some way. word:lxx:L705437.explanation: Ermōni is a proper name, rendered “Ermōni” or “Ermoni,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705442.explanation: This verb means “crawl,” describing movement close to the ground rather than ordinary walking or running. word:lxx:L705558.explanation: This noun refers to nobility of birth or high descent—an honorable standing connected with a person’s family origin. word:lxx:L705653.explanation: Euodos means easy to pass. It can describe a way that goes well.

word:lxx:L705851.explanation: Zaō means to live or be alive.

word:lxx:L706025.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “hero,” referring to a person regarded as unusually brave, strong, or distinguished. word:lxx:L707228.explanation: This noun refers to thinking ill of someone or regarding that person as low. It describes a negative judgment or low estimation of another person. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Sirach 5:14. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning centers on holding another person in low regard or thinking badly of them.

word:lxx:L707264.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to the ashes left from a burnt sacrifice. It names the material residue of something consumed by fire, rather than the offering itself or the act of burning. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Leviticus 6:3–4. Its precise use in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains specific: ashes associated with a burnt sacrifice.

word:lxx:L707361.explanation: This word means “trampling” or “treading”—the act of stepping forcefully on something or walking over it. It is a noun that describes such an action, and it can also function adjectivally to characterize something marked by trampling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times across ten verses, including passages in Isaiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, Lamentations, and Micah. Its central idea remains the physical action of being trodden down or walked upon; the surrounding verse determines whether the word describes an act, condition, or image.

word:lxx:L707383.explanation: “Wear down” is a verb describing the act of making someone or something weaker, more exhausted, or less able to continue. It focuses on the effect of continued pressure, difficulty, or exertion rather than on a single moment. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, at 2:2 and 2:13. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L707475.explanation: Kataphthora means destruction. It can also mean death.

word:lxx:L707729.explanation: “By lot” means in a manner determined by casting or using lots, rather than by ordinary choice or personal assignment. It is an adverb, so it describes how an action or distribution takes place. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word appears four times, all in Joshua 21, where the surrounding passage concerns the distribution of designated cities. The word itself states the method—by lot—while the passage supplies the particular outcome.

word:lxx:L707750.explanation: This noun means the part of the body between the knee and ankle—the lower leg. It refers to a physical body part and may be rendered simply as “leg” when describing a person’s limbs. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs five times, appearing in Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalms, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L707822.explanation: Kopē means cutting down or slaughter.

word:lxx:L707934.explanation: This noun means “livestock” or “animal,” referring generally to a living creature kept, counted, or discussed as property. It is a broad word rather than the name of one particular species. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs 246 times, showing regular use in descriptions of created creatures, household or owned animals, and animals included in ordinary laws and accounts. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707978.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “dog fly,” referring to a kind of fly. It names an insect rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, with most occurrences in Exodus and additional occurrences in Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the name of this fly.

word:lxx:L707996.explanation: Kyrios means lord or master. In one setting, a servant uses this title for a human superior by saying “my lord.” It can also refer to Yahweh, the God of Israel, when he is addressed in prayer.

word:lxx:L708063.explanation: Lais, also rendered Les, is a proper name—a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 25:44. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself identifies a person or named figure, while the passage supplies the details about whom it refers to. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name “Lais” or “Les,” not an abstract idea or general description.

word:lxx:L708081.explanation: This adjective means “like a covered chariot” or “covered.” It describes something having a covering or resembling a covered vehicle. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 7:3, so its normal meaning is shown by this single recorded use rather than by a broad range of passages. The word itself describes a quality or appearance; the surrounding verse determines exactly what object it modifies there.

word:lxx:L708166.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “whiteness,” referring to the quality or appearance of being white. It names a visible characteristic rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Sirach 43:18. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being white or pale in appearance.

word:lxx:L708232.explanation: This word means to account for something or count it—that is, to assess, reckon, or regard it in a particular way. As a verb, it describes the act of treating something as having a certain value or standing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 110 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through the later writings, so it serves a broad purpose in describing how people or God evaluate, calculate, or regard matters. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L708247.explanation: Loipon means the remainder, or what is left.

word:lxx:L708430.explanation: Makchi, also rendered Makkhi, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek LXX text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Numbers 13:15. The available lexical information establishes the name and its identity, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in that passage.

word:lxx:L708449.explanation: Mallo is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 12:21. The name itself does not reveal the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the surrounding verse and passage. Here, Mallo functions simply as a personal name.

word:lxx:L708485.explanation: This adjective describes something as “like madness” or “mad.” It points to behavior, speech, or a condition that appears irrational or out of control, rather than calm and sensible. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 5:45. That single occurrence establishes its basic descriptive function, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what person or action it describes there. Its central idea remains the appearance or reality of madness.

word:lxx:L708504.explanation: Marēsa is a proper name, also represented as “Marisa.” It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:21. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its particular referent cannot be identified beyond this naming function. The name itself should therefore be read as a designation, with the passage supplying the specific person or place intended.

word:lxx:L708548.explanation: Maserephōthmaim, also rendered Maserefothmem, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 13:6. Since the available record identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text or a further definition, its basic meaning is the name itself; its precise referent is established by the context of Joshua 13:6.

word:lxx:L708636.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “boast” or describes someone as a “boaster.” It expresses proud, self-important speech rather than humble or modest words. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Ezekiel 35:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the context there. Its basic sense remains speech marked by boasting or proud self-assertion.

word:lxx:L708694.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “blacken” or “become black.” It describes a change in color toward blackness, whether something is made dark or grows dark. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Song of Songs and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the darkening or blackening of something.

word:lxx:L708845.explanation: “Moderately” describes something done or present to a limited, balanced, or not extreme degree. As an adverb, the word modifies an action or description by showing its extent rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:38. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a measured degree rather than excess or intensity.

word:lxx:L708889.explanation: “Mērōz” or “Miroz” is a proper name, rendered as Meroz in Judges 5:23. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs only once, at Judges 5:23. The name itself does not provide a broader lexical definition; understanding its particular reference requires the verse and its surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L708971.explanation: This adjective describes someone who can hardly speak or is unable to speak. It points to impaired or absent speech rather than expressing a general idea about silence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 35:6, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains a person who is speech-impaired or dumb.

word:lxx:L708993.explanation: Moni is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 18:24, and is rendered “Moni.” Because the supplied material does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it does not establish more about whom or what Moni identifies. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context of Joshua 18:24.

word:lxx:L709099.explanation: A welt is a raised mark or swelling on the body, ordinarily associated with an injury. It is a noun naming the visible result of a blow or wound rather than the action itself. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a welt: an outward bodily mark caused by harm.

word:lxx:L709107.explanation: This verb means “make foolish” or “turn into foolishness.” It describes causing someone or something to become foolish rather than merely identifying foolishness as a quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 44:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an action that produces foolishness or renders something foolish.

word:lxx:L709226.explanation: Nachoth is a proper name, rendered as “Nachoth” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but as the identifying name itself. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Genesis 36:13 and Genesis 36:17. The available lexical definition gives “Nachoth; Nakhoth,” preserving the name rather than translating it into an ordinary English meaning.

word:lxx:L709284.explanation: Nechaō is the name Nechao, referring to Pharaoh Nechao, king of Egypt.

word:lxx:L709341.explanation: The word means “lawfully.” As an adverb, it describes how an action is performed—according to law or in a lawful manner. Its basic focus is not the person acting but the character of the action: the action conforms to law. Within this LXX usage, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 6:18; the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific force there.

word:lxx:L709459.explanation: Odouia, also rendered Othoia, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Chronicles 3:24 and once in Nehemiah 10:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the person’s family, role, or historical importance; those details belong to the passages where it appears.

word:lxx:L709495.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “make one’s own”: to take something or someone as belonging to oneself. It describes an act of claiming, adopting, or treating something as one’s own rather than merely observing or encountering it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:26. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of making something one’s own.

word:lxx:L709778.explanation: Orphanhood means the condition of being without parents or parental care. As a noun, it names that state of loss and vulnerability rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 47:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of orphanhood. The word therefore points to the experience or status of those left without the protection and care normally provided by parents.

word:lxx:L709873.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “bitten by a snake.” It identifies the condition caused by a snake’s bite, rather than naming the snake itself or describing a general danger. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 12:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the context, but its basic meaning remains clear: affected by a snake bite.

word:lxx:L709929.explanation: This verb means “beget children”—to father or bring children into being. It describes the act of producing offspring rather than simply referring to children themselves. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:25. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific force there, but the word’s basic meaning remains the act of begetting children.

word:lxx:L709950.explanation: This adjective describes something as “all-mingled; promiscuous”—mixed together without clear separation or distinction. It can describe a condition in which different people or things are gathered into one mixture rather than kept apart. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is complete or indiscriminate mingling.

word:lxx:L710013.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “embrace” or “admit”—to receive someone or something willingly, or to accept it as true or acceptable. It describes an active response rather than merely noticing or encountering something. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Exodus, Proverbs, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

word:lxx:L710109.explanation: This verb means “stretch along,” describing an action in which something extends lengthwise along a line or area. It focuses on the way something reaches outward or continues across a space, rather than naming an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, each in a different verse. Its central meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding passage determines what is being extended and how that action functions in the sentence.

word:lxx:L710170.explanation: This Greek verb means to urge someone forward or stimulate them to action. It describes active encouragement that moves a person toward doing something, rather than merely expressing approval or giving information. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 15:17 and 4 Maccabees 12:6. Since the surrounding verse text is not included, those references establish where it appears but do not determine the specific nuance in either passage.

word:lxx:L710277.explanation: This word means “bake.” It is a verb describing the act of preparing food by baking it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, at Leviticus 6:10 and Leviticus 23:17. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: something is made ready through baking. The surrounding words determine what is being baked and how the action functions in each passage, but the word itself refers to the baking process rather than to a person, object, or abstract idea.

word:lxx:L710318.explanation: This noun refers to a cover or wrapping—something placed around or over another object. It describes a physical covering rather than an action or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the books of Numbers and Judges. The exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being covered and the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a material cover or wrapping.

word:lxx:L710354.explanation: Perioikodomeō means to build around something.

word:lxx:L710431.explanation: Persis is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times: once in Daniel and nine times in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise reference must be determined from each passage. The name appears in Daniel 11:2 and in several passages in 1 Maccabees.

word:lxx:L710606.explanation: This verb means “maintain war with” or “keep up war.” It describes continuing or sustaining a conflict rather than merely beginning one. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees, where its subject is presented as persisting in warfare. The word therefore focuses on the ongoing character of military conflict. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being described.

word:lxx:L710743.explanation: This noun refers to an evergreen oak, specifically an ilex, a type of tree that remains green throughout the year. Its meaning is botanical and concrete: it identifies the tree itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Susanna 1:58. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact role in that sentence must be understood from that passage’s context.

word:lxx:L710835.explanation: This LXX verb means “dispatch ahead” or “send forth.” It describes sending someone or something onward, often with the idea of going before or being sent out for a purpose. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or quality. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is sending forth or arranging for someone to go ahead.

word:lxx:L710880.explanation: This noun refers to “besieging” or “assiduity”—persistent, sustained attention or effort. It can describe pressing upon someone continually, whether in an adverse sense such as a siege or in the broader sense of devoted persistence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:15. Without the verse text, its precise force in that passage cannot be stated more narrowly, but its central idea is continued pressure or steadfast application rather than a brief or casual action.

word:lxx:L710927.explanation: This verb means to stoop to, describing a downward bending or lowering oneself toward something. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:27. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific action in that passage. Its central meaning remains the act of stooping or bending toward something.

word:lxx:L710952.explanation: Prospiptō means to fall at someone’s feet. It can also describe falling against someone.

word:lxx:L711061.explanation: This adjective describes someone suffering from an eyelid disease, with the eyelids inflamed. It is a specific physical description rather than a general word for sickness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 21:20. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: a person affected by diseased or inflamed eyelids.

word:lxx:L711128.explanation: Raau, also rendered Rhaav, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:30, identifying a person or place by name. The name itself does not carry an additional meaning in the available material, and its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L711300.explanation: Roōb, also rendered Rhoov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or place named Roōb. The name appears three times, in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here, but its basic function remains that of a personal or place name. The spelling may appear slightly differently in English because transliteration represents the Greek name rather than translating it.

word:lxx:L711379.explanation: Sathour, also rendered Sathur, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it appears once, at Numbers 13:13. The available lexical information identifies it as the name itself, without providing an additional meaning or definition. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the person being named.

word:lxx:L711429.explanation: Salomoth is a proper name, referring to a person named Salomoth rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears six times across five verses, all in 1 Chronicles. Since it is a personal name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes this individual from other people mentioned in genealogical and service records. The name is rendered consistently as “Salomoth.”

word:lxx:L711450.explanation: This proper noun refers to a Samaritan, a person identified with Samaria. Its lexical gloss is “Samareitēs; Samaritis,” naming the person rather than describing an action, quality, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:29. Because the word is a name for a people or person associated with Samaria, the surrounding verse supplies the particular setting in which it is used. It should therefore be understood primarily as an identifying name.

word:lxx:L711573.explanation: Saphat, also written Safat, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament and is preserved as a name in English translation. This name appears four times in the LXX, across four verses. Its significance in any particular passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding account, not from a separate definition attached to the name.

word:lxx:L711656.explanation: Sellēsa is a proper name, also represented as Sellisa. It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 16:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its identity as the name Sellēsa or Sellisa.

word:lxx:L711920.explanation: Sodoma is a place-name for a city.

word:lxx:L711995.explanation: This noun means “swathing band,” a strip or band used to wrap an infant or person. It names a practical piece of cloth rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Ezekiel and once in Wisdom. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself refers plainly to a band used for wrapping or binding.

word:lxx:L712020.explanation: In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this noun means “heap of ashes” or “ashes.” It refers to the remains left after something has been burned, especially when gathered into a pile. The word appears four times in the LXX, in Leviticus and Numbers, and its English rendering is consistently “ashes.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L712059.explanation: This verb means to “cover” or “resist,” describing an action of shielding something or standing against what is happening. It can therefore express either protection or opposition, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Sirach 8:17. The word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains the ability to cover or withstand. Its meaning is expressed directly as “cover; resist.”

word:lxx:L712095.explanation: This noun means “warp,” the set of threads arranged lengthwise in woven cloth. It names part of a textile rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, all in Leviticus 13, where the surrounding subject is cloth being examined. Its basic meaning remains the textile structure called the warp; the precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L712222.explanation: This adjective means “shut up,” describing something closed, confined, or prevented from being open or accessible. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 7:36. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this basic sense. Its central idea is being shut in or closed off rather than open or freely available.

word:lxx:L712257.explanation: This noun describes a false accuser or slanderer—someone who brings damaging charges or speaks against another without truth. It names a person rather than the act of accusing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, in Psalms and Proverbs, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse wording is not provided here. The word points to harmful, unjust speech that misrepresents another person.

word:lxx:L712334.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “twine together”: to combine separate strands or parts by winding or intertwining them. It describes an action that brings things into a joined whole, rather than leaving them separate. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Job, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being joined there.

word:lxx:L712378.explanation: Synathroizō means to gather together or collect.

word:lxx:L712396.explanation: Synantēma means an event or fate, referring to what happens or befalls someone.

word:lxx:L712455.explanation: This verb means “work with” or “work together.” It describes acting alongside another person or group so that a task or purpose is shared rather than carried out alone. The word’s basic idea is cooperation: people contribute together toward an undertaking. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:1; the surrounding verse text is not available, so its broader role there cannot be described more specifically.

word:lxx:L712507.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “throw all together into confusion” or “confound.” It describes causing people or circumstances to become confused, disturbed, or thrown into disorder. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Old Testament books and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L712572.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “thong,” referring to a narrow strip or band of material. It is used seven times in the Greek Old Testament, including descriptions of the lampstand and its connected parts in Exodus 25. The word therefore identifies a physical strip or band used as part of an object, rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description of the object.

word:lxx:L712684.explanation: Tabek, also rendered Tavek, is a proper name. It identifies a person or named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Genesis 22:24. The available lexical definition preserves the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description. Its precise role in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the person named there.

word:lxx:L712741.explanation: This noun refers to a ditch or trench—a dug channel or depression in the ground. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Micah 5:5. Its basic meaning describes a physical feature of the land rather than an action or personal quality. The surrounding verse is needed to determine its particular significance there, but the word itself points plainly to a trench or ditch.

word:lxx:L712828.explanation: Tephōn, also rendered Tefon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 9:50. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity; its precise identification must come from that passage’s context.

word:lxx:L712864.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “shake,” referring to a shaking or trembling movement. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 28:26. The word names the movement itself rather than describing a person or action in detail. Its precise force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a shake or act of shaking.

word:lxx:L712961.explanation: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “do for the third time”. It describes an action repeated until it has occurred three times. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Kings 18:34. The word therefore focuses on repetition and the completion of a third performance, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific action being repeated.

word:lxx:L712983.explanation: This verb means to serve as a wet nurse—to nurse and care for an infant. It describes the practical act of feeding and tending a child, rather than a general reference to teaching or upbringing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Exodus and once in Baruch. Its ordinary sense remains focused on nursing a child. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L713153.explanation: This noun means “contempt; disdain”: a despising attitude that treats someone or something as beneath regard. It names an attitude rather than an action, so the word points to the way a person regards another. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 22:30. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an expression of contempt or disdain.

word:lxx:L713214.explanation: This noun refers to an “under-trough” or “vat,” a container positioned beneath something to hold liquid. It names a physical vessel rather than an action or quality.
